paper_title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.

sections.content: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos? Jun Wang Haoyu Zhao Zafeirios Fountas University College London Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the models reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning. 1. Introduction Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents have demonstrated impressive capabilities across wide range of domains [14]. Yet under conventional parametric learning, their capabilities are largely fixed once training is complete, and enabling such systems to improve continually after deployment remains central challenge [5, 6]. Updating these models typically requires training signals from humanlabeled data or environmental feedback [7, 8], yet repeated fine-tuning is prohibitively expensive at scale. Humans, by contrast, routinely learn from instructional materials such as books and tutorial videos [9, 10]. Millions of new instructional videos are uploaded online every day [11], creating rapidly growing multimodal resource that todays LLM agents cannot yet fully leverage. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? One promising direction is the recent line of nonparametric mechanisms for LLM agents [5, 6, 8], in which capability is grown through external memory rather than continual weight updates. As summarized in Fig. 1, this line splits into two forms. In the first, knowledge is supplied externally by humans, as in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [12] and agent skills [13]. RAG retrieves textual evidence from human-curated corpora, while agent skills inject human-authored workflows specified in structured formats such as markdown. These approaches are effective, but they rely on knowledge manually curated for agent consumption and therefore do not scale with the open-world supply of human teaching. In the second form, knowledge is derived from the models own past interactions, as in case-based reasoning (CBR) [14], where adaptation proceeds by retrieving similar prior cases. Because such memory records what happened rather than why or how, CBR offers limited interpretive guidance in novel contexts, and its effectiveness depends heavily on case coverage and the models ability to reason from raw trajectories.

sections.title: These limitations motivate a third direction in which agents learn reusable knowledge from tutorial
sections.content: Corresponding author: jun.wang@cs.ucl.ac.uk 1 Figure 1: Overview of learning paradigms for LLM agents, comparing parametric and non-parametric approaches along the dimensions of stored knowledge, inference-time usage, and update mechanism. videos. Unlike curated RAG corpora and hand-crafted skills, tutorial videos already exist at internet scale and require no agent-specific curation; unlike case-based experience, they do not merely record what happened, but pair demonstrations with explanations of why and how, providing direct interpretive guidance for future reasoning. Yet todays LLM agents lack mechanism to convert raw tutorial videos into persistent, reusable knowledge. Videos are information-rich, inherently multimodal, making this conversion nontrivial. If such structured knowledge could be consolidated from tutorial videos and organized for reuse, an agent could improve from human teaching without modifying its parameters. To realize this, we introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into structured tutorial memorya tutorialbookthat frozen LLM can read at inference time. TAL learns this memory through two-stage consolidation. Stage harvests hard, video-grounded questions: video agent generates questionanswer pairs supported by evidence, and only those the frozen model fails to answer without external context are retained. Stage II turns these failures into targeted memory edits via readwrite loop: TAL revisits the relevant tutorial context, validates the missing knowledge exposed by each failure, and rewrites the corresponding chapters to incorporate the missing knowledge. At inference time, TAL retrieves through Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree: the model first scans the chapter titles to identify relevant chapters, then expands those chapters to access the underlying details. This ties retrieval to the models reasoning rather than to embedding similarity, eliminating the mismatch between semantic similarity and task relevance. TAL generalizes beyond both RAG-style evidence lookup and case-level replay by turning human teaching videos into an external knowledge structure that can be incrementally refined and reused. To study this setting, we construct VidLearn, multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 classical openings. Chess offers controlled yet realistic testbed by combining struc2 tured knowledge, an abundant supply of online tutorials, rich visuallanguage grounding, and nontrivial multi-step reasoning. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms strong fine-tuning-free baselines by up to 113% on the training split and 91% on the test split, and the learned memory transfers to actual play, where TAL reaches stronger opening-phase position than the vanilla baseline in 69% of head-to-head games, as evaluated by Stockfish. Crucially, TALs performance scales monotonically with the number of consumed tutorial videos, demonstrating that frozen LLM agents can continuously accumulate reusable knowledge from instructional videos without parameter updates. To assess cross-domain generalization, we additionally evaluate TAL in software-tutorial setting. Across matched comparisons with stronger retrieval and memory baselines, TAL achieves the highest mean accuracy in all eight chess settings and reaches 49.7% held-out accuracy in the software domain, 10.9 percentage points above the strongest baseline. Our main contributions are: We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that enables frozen LLM agents to learn from instructional videos without parameter updates. We design two-stage adversarial consolidation that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine structured tutorial memory, together with TOC-based retrieval mechanism that ties inference-time retrieval to the models own reasoning. We introduce VidLearn, benchmark of 72 chess tutorial videos across 12 openings, and provide extensive evaluations on VidLearn and separate software-tutorial setting, demonstrating TALs effectiveness, scalability, and cross-domain generalization. 2. Related Work 2.1. Continual Learning for LLM Agents growing body of work enables LLM agents to improve from experience without fine-tuning, relying on external memory rather than parameter updates [1521]. These efforts fall into two paradigms. Skillbased methods [13, 22, 23] store reusable workflows for on-demand invocation, but constructing highquality workflows often requires manual curation, limiting their scalability to online instructional resources. Experience-based methods, rooted in case-based reasoning [14, 24] and exemplified by recent systems such as Memento [25, 26], store and retrieve prior agent-generated cases through reflective read write loops. Related reflection-based methods, such as Reflexion [27] and Self-Refine [28], use failures or feedback to iteratively improve individual trajectories or outputs. While effective, case-level reuse depends on the availability of similar past interactions and on the models ability to reason from retrieved cases. TAL departs from both by consolidating knowledge from human tutorial videos into structured, reusable knowledge substrate. 2.2. Learning from Demonstrations Learning from human demonstrations has long been central theme in robotics [2932], where agents learn by imitating expert trajectories. However, demonstrations in these settings are typically distilled into policies or action sequences for task execution and control [33, 34] rather than into reusable knowledge structures. More recently, multimodal LLM research has targeted long-form single-video understanding [3537], where models struggle as videos grow longer and denser. Retrieval-augmented approaches such as VideoRAG [3840] and in-context methods such as Demo-ICL [41] address this by retrieving relevant segments before generation. Yet these works primarily target inference-time comprehen3 Figure 2: Overview of Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL). In Stage I, TAL performs video-grounded agent model adversarial consolidation, where video agent harvests hard questionanswer pairs from instructional videos that are supported by tutorial evidence yet unsolved by the frozen model, forming question bank. In Stage II, TAL performs questionmemory adversarial consolidation, using this question bank to iteratively refine tutorial memory through readwrite loop. At inference time, TAL retrieves relevant tutorial units via Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, enabling the frozen model to access structured tutorial knowledge for downstream reasoning without parameter updates. sion of individual videos, whereas TAL converts tutorial videos into structured external knowledge that frozen LLM agents can reuse across future tasks. 3. Tutorialbook Memory as Learning Substrate We contrast three learning substrates: (1) Parametric learning, where knowledge is implicitly stored in model parameters and adaptation is achieved through weight updates. (2) Case-level replay, where adaptation is achieved by retrieving stored episodic cases, typically produced by the agents own interactions, while keeping the model frozen. (3) TAL tutorial memory, also referred to as tutorialbook, where adaptation is achieved by writing and reading structured knowledge consolidated from multimodal human tutorials without changing model weights. TAL therefore shifts the learning substrate from parameter space or raw episodic traces to an evolving tutorialbook memory that consolidates multimodal tutorial content with its supporting evidence into reusable tutorialbook: (r) = {(kj, (r) (r) )}N j=1 , (1) (R) where {0, 1, . . . , R} denotes the refinement round, is the total number of rounds, is the final (r) refined memory, kj is the chapters retrieval key (category, title, and short summary), and is textbookj style chapter with an overview, thematic sections (each elaborated by bullet points and key terms), and summary that consolidates the takeaways. 3.2. Two-Stage Adversarial Consolidation TAL learns tutorial memory through two-stage adversarial consolidation: Stage harvests hard, videogrounded questions exposing the frozen models gaps, and Stage II turns these failures into targeted memory edits via readwrite loop [25]. We detail each stage below. 3.2.1. Stage I: Video-Grounded AgentModel Adversarial Consolidation Stage constructs the hard question bank used to supervise tutorial-memory refinement in Stage II. To do so, TAL instantiates video-grounded agentmodel adversarial process over each video. video agent analyzes aligned visual and textual evidence to generate candidate questions, while the frozen solver attempts to answer them without external context. The goal is to retain questions that are both supported by the tutorial evidence and difficult for the frozen model. For each tutorial video, the video agent parses the video and subtitles, aligns multimodal evidence by timestamp, and samples an evidence snippet = (τ, Wτ, Iτ) from the video. Concretely, each snippet consists of (i) timestamp anchor τ chosen by the planner from the subtitle timeline, (ii) the local subtitle window Wτ spanning 10 neighborhood of τ, and (iii) the video frame Iτ extracted at τ; together they pin single teaching moment to specific (text, vision) pair. The agent then generates grounded question Gϕ(vt, e) via question generator Gϕ (where ϕ is updated each round through reflective revision of easy-question failures), derives reference answer from e, and forms multimodal query xq pairing with Iτ. TOC Retrieval (R) TAL instantiates Read(x, ) through Table-of-Contents (TOC) retrieval mechanism mirroring how humans use book: skim the index, decide which chapters to read, then expand only those chapters in detail. The tutorial memory is structured as hierarchical TOC tree of volumes, parts, and chapters (the atomic content units). Retrieval is thus driven by the LLMs reasoning rather than 4. Experiment 4.1. Dataset We use chess as controlled yet realistic testbed for learning from instructional videos. Chess offers four advantages for this purpose: (i) well-codified body of teachable knowledge developed over centuries [45]; (ii) an abundant supply of tutorial videos on YouTube, providing scalable supervision; (iii) multimodal instruction that pairs visual board states with natural-language explanations; and (iv) substantial difficulty for current LLMs [46, 47], leaving room for measurable progress. Based on these properties, we introduce VidLearn, benchmark of 72 tutorial videos spanning 12 classical openings (Appendix B). For each opening, we collect six videos via YouTube search using the opening name as the query. The benchmark contains 48 training videos and 110 multimodal test questions derived from 24 held-out videos, with all test annotations manually verified. During training, the agent is given only the YouTube links. At test time, it answers each question using only single video frame, natural-language query, and multiple-choice options. 4.2. Experimental Setup We use two complementary evaluation protocols. First, to assess robustness across model families, we compare four methods: (i) vanilla direct prompting, (ii) prompting with thinking mode enabled, (iii) Transcript-RAG, and (iv) TAL. All four methods are evaluated across four different model families, including GPT-5.2 [48], Kimi K2.5 [49], Gemini 3 Flash [50], and Claude Sonnet 4.6 [51]. Second, to compare TAL with stronger retrieval and memory systems under matched setting, we fix the backbone to Gemini-3.5-Flash [52] at temperature 0.7 and evaluate vanilla prompting, Transcript-RAG, two VideoRAG variants [38], mem0 [17], ReasoningBank [19], and TAL. Full implementation details are provided in Appendix A.1. 8 Table 1: Comparison of baseline methods and TAL on the training and test sets under varying numbers of demonstration videos. Best results are in bold. TAL consistently outperforms all baselines across all settings, showing clear scaling trend as more tutorial demonstrations become available.

Each round segments the tutorial timeline into 20 event candidates, each anchored to timestamped frame and its surrounding subtitles. It then generates one question per event. We cap harvesting at 60 questions per video to ensure broad temporal coverage while avoiding diminishing returns from long-tail mining. In Stage II, memory refinement runs for at most three iterations, with early stopping based on validation performance. At inference, TOC retrieval selects the top three chapters as tutorial evidence. For consistency, all cross-model TAL experiments use the same GPT-5.2-generated tutorialbook, allowing us to evaluate whether the learned tutorial memory transfers across models. 4.3. Main Results During Stage I, TAL harvests 174 multimodal QA instances from the 48 training videos, which serve as the question bank Qbank for Stage II memory refinement. We report accuracy on these harvested questions to measure how much of the targeted knowledge TAL successfully absorbs into memory, and on the heldout test set to measure generalization to unseen videos. Table 1 summarizes the main results. Overall, TAL achieves the best performance on both splits and exhibits the strongest scaling behavior with respect to the number of tutorial videos. Relative to the corresponding vanilla MLLM baselines, TAL attains maximum relative gain of 112.72% on the training set (GPT-5.2) and 91.42% on the test set (Kimi K2.5), showing that frozen LLM agents can substantially benefit from instructional videos without any parameter updates. 9 key pattern in Table 1 is the contrast between TAL and the other fine-tuning-free baselines as the training corpus grows. RAG improves training performance by exposing the model to subtitle evidence, but its gains on the test set are inconsistent and often deteriorate at larger corpus sizes. By contrast, TAL continues to improve as more tutorial videos are added. This suggests that retrieval over raw subtitle chunks becomes increasingly noisy with scale, making it harder to surface evidence that is genuinely useful for reasoning. Enabling the models built-in thinking mode also fails to yield consistent improvements over direct answering, and in some cases performs slightly worse. Taken together, these results indicate that the main bottleneck in this setting is not simply inference-time reasoning depth, but access to the right instructional knowledge. TAL specifically addresses this bottleneck via structured tutorial memory and TOC retrieval. Ability Scaling. TAL leads at every video budget, and its advantage widens monotonically with corpus size  (Fig. 3)  : each additional tutorial is consolidated into progressively richer memory with broader topical coverage, so that TAL accumulates reusable knowledge over time rather than merely caching individual demonstrations. The resulting trajectory mirrors human-like learning curve, for which we provide reference under the same setting in Appendix C. Beyond accuracy, TAL also yields much more compact knowledge representation: with 48 training videos, the raw subtitle corpus used by RAG contains 598,027 tokens, whereas the resulting tutorial memory contains only 105,703 tokensan 82.32% reduction, while still delivering higher accuracy on both splits. Figure 3: Scaling behavior of TAL vs. vanilla (GPT-5.2) on training (left) and test (right) splits. Cross-Model Transferability. Beyond scaling, TAL improves performance across all four model families, indicating that its gains are not tied to any single answer model. The tutorial memory built by GPT-5.2 can be consumed directly by other LLMs at inference via TOC retrieval, without rebuilding, suggesting that TAL externalizes instructional knowledge in model-agnostic form that can be built once and reused across answer models. Comparison with Retrieval and Memory Baselines. We further compare TAL against two Video-RAG variants [38] and two recent text-based memory systems, mem0 [17] and ReasoningBank [19]. All methods use the same Gemini-3.5-Flash backbone at temperature 0.7, with results reported as meanstandard deviation over three seeds. Implementation details are provided in Appendix A.1. As shown in Table 2, TAL achieves the highest mean accuracy in all eight training/test settings. With 48 videos, it reaches 84.1% on the training questions and 71.8% on the held-out set, compared with 64.6% and 64.5% for the strongest respective baselines. 10 Table 2: Comparison with stronger retrieval and memory baselines. TALs question harvesting, memory refinement, and TOC retrieval do not rely on chess-specific representations. To assess cross-domain generalization, we apply TAL to software tutorials covering four Adobe Photoshop 2026 features: Generative Fill, Harmonize, Object Removal & Selection, and AI Adjustments & Workspace. Following the same evaluation protocol as in the main VidLearn experiments, we collect 28 videos, using 16 for learning and holding out 12 for evaluation, and construct 108 QA pairs comprising 53 training questions and 55 held-out test questions. We compare TAL with Vanilla, Transcript-RAG, two Video-RAG variants [38], mem0 [17], and ReasoningBank [19]. All methods use Gemini-3.5-Flash at temperature 0.7, and we report meanstandard deviation over three seeds. Table 3: Second-domain evaluation on Adobe Photoshop 2026 software tutorials. Best results are in bold. Method Training Set (53 QA) Test Set (55 QA) # Demonstration Videos 4 8 16 4 8 12 16 Vanilla (no memory) 38.45.4 21.23.7 62.32.7 66.70.9 72.30.9 78.60.9 27.32.6 35.80.9 29.73.1 30.92.6 Transcript-RAG 68.60.9 72.32.4 81.80.9 84.33.2 33.90.9 38.28.3 29.73.1 38.84.8 Video-RAG (caption retrieval) [38] Video-RAG (+retrieved frames) [38] 67.31.8 74.83.2 84.30.9 86.21.8 32.10.9 36.41.5 27.31.5 33.92.3 54.13.6 57.20.9 67.91.5 71.71.5 29.75.6 33.91.7 33.94.8 33.91.7 mem0 [17] 46.53.2 45.32.7 45.96.4 49.71.8 24.23.1 24.85.6 23.04.5 27.92.3 ReasoningBank [19] 69.23.9 82.40.9 96.21.5 98.70.9 32.10.8 40.01.5 35.83.7 49.75.2 TAL (ours) As the training corpus grows from 4 to 16 videos, TALs training accuracy increases from 69.2% to 98.7%  (Table 3)  . With all 16 training videos, TAL reaches 49.7% on held-out questions, 10.9 percentage points above the strongest baseline. TAL obtains the highest mean in all four training settings and in three of the four held-out settings, demonstrating TALs effectiveness across domains. 4.4. Head-to-Head Evaluation To evaluate whether TAL improves practical move-level decision quality in direct play, we construct controlled head-to-head chess environment. In this setting, both agents use the same base model (GPT5.2): vanilla agent that plays from model priors alone, and TAL agent that plays with tutorial-memory retrieval enabled. We evaluate all 12 openings covered by VidLearn. For each opening, games begin from fixed opening-specific position. To reduce side bias, we adopt color-swapped protocol and run 20 games per opening (10 each as White and Black). 11 We assess opening-phase quality at move horizons {2, 3, 4, 5} using two metrics: (1) Win rate: at the move-N cutoff, the side with the higher Stockfish evaluation is credited with win (draws count as 0.5), and we aggregate win rates across all games. This metric captures which agent obtains the more favorable position after fixed number of moves. (2) Average CentiPawn Loss (ACPL): we compute the per-move deviation of each sides played move from the Stockfish-optimal move (one pawn = 100 centipawns); lower values indicate higher move quality. As shown in Table 4, TAL achieves higher win rates and lower ACPL than the vanilla baseline at every horizon, indicating that tutorial memory translates into measurably better move-level decisions in practical play. Table 4: Head-to-head TAL vs. vanilla results under fixed openings. Horizon Win Rate (TAL/Van) Mean ACPL (TAL/Van) Median ACPL (TAL/Van) 5% Trimmed Mean ACPL (TAL/Van) move2 move3 move4 move 50.83% / 49.17% 69.17% / 30.83% 67.92% / 32.08% 62.50% / 37.50% 63.14 / 85.26 87.62 / 142.98 107.34 / 153.51 125.74 / 162.81 11.50 / 24.50 28.83 / 135.17 66.25 / 146.75 112.60 / 156.60 47.98 / 74.36 75.01 / 130.75 99.96 / 145.38 119.24 / 159.01 4.5. Ablation Study 4.5.1. Effect of Two-Stage Consolidation To isolate the contribution of each stage, we evaluate two reduced variants. Stage only uses the harvested QA pairs directly as case memory at inference time, reducing TAL to case-based reasoning (CBR)-style system. Stage II only retains the initial tutorialbook constructed from video but disables Stage II refinement against the harvested question bank. Both stages contribute substantially  (Table 5)  : Stage only improves over vanilla from 48.18% to 55.45%, while Stage II only reaches similar 56.36%. Full TAL reaches 71.82%, 8.2 points above the additive prediction of 63.63%, suggesting that the two stages interact synergistically. 4.5.2. Effect of Retrieval Strategy We isolate the retrieval mechanism via 12-way opening classification: strategy is correct if its top3 retrieved chapters include the querys source opening. With the tutorialbook and base model fixed, TOC retrieval achieves 50.00% Recall@3, compared with 28.18% for dense retrieval using OpenAIs textembedding-3-small  (Table 6)  . This 21.82-point improvement indicates that reasoning over the tutorialbook structure better captures opening-level relevance than embedding similarity. Table 5: Two-stage consolidation ablation. Table 6: Retrieval-strategy ablation. Setting Stage Stage II Test Score Setting Recall@3 Vanilla Setting Stage only (w/ CBR, w/o Tutorialbook) Stage II only (w/ Tutorialbook, w/o Refinement) Stage + Stage II (Full TAL) No Yes No Yes No No Yes Yes 48.18% 55.45% 56.36% 71.82% TAL + Embedding Retrieval TAL + TOC Retrieval 28.18% 50.00% 4.5.3. Effect of Visual Information To isolate whether visual information contributes during tutorial-memory construction, we compare two otherwise matched TAL variants on the same 110 held-out questions. Full TAL constructs the tutorialbook from event-aligned video frames and transcripts, whereas transcript-only TAL removes all visual inputs and constructs the tutorialbook solely from subtitle text. We use Gemini-3.5-Flash answer model at temperature 0.7 and report the mean and standard deviation over three seeds. Table 7: Vision-in-construction ablation on 110 held-out questions. Full TAL uses event-aligned frames and transcripts, while transcript-only TAL removes all visual inputs. Results are meanstandard deviation over three seeds; best results are in bold. Memory built from Test accuracy (%) at # demonstration videos Vanilla (no memory) Transcript-only TAL (no visual input) Full TAL (frames + transcripts) 57.62.3 58.81.4 64.52.0 58.52.3 64.81.1 60.95.5 66.10.4 62.11.9 71.82.0 24 36 48 Full TAL outperforms transcript-only TAL at every video budget, reaching 71.8% versus 62.1% with 48 videos. During memory construction and refinement, event-aligned framesubtitle pairs connect the lecturers explanation to concrete board states, pieces, squares, and spatial relations. Because the TAL pipeline is otherwise held fixed, this comparison directly isolates the contribution of visual evidence rather than differences in retrieval or memory design. This consistent advantage shows that TAL leverages visual information during learning, supporting the complementary value of tutorial videos beyond their transcripts. 4.5.4. Impact of Retrieval Depth Table 8 reveals crossover between = 3 and = 5 as the tutorial corpus grows. With sparse memory (12 24 videos), = 5 outperforms = 3 by 2.73.6 points, as additional retrieved chapters help compensate for the limited per-query coverage of an immature tutorialbook. Once memory matures past 24 videos, the ranking flips: at 48 videos, = 3 reaches 71.82% while = 5 reaches only 66.36%. We attribute this to coveragedilution tradeoff: when individual chapters are already information-dense, surfacing additional ones increasingly introduces marginally relevant content rather than new evidence. Table 8: Impact of retrieval depth. Setting # Demonstration Videos Top-k = 3 = 5 24 36 48 54.55% 57.27% 69.09% 71.82% 58.18% 60.00% 60.91% 66.36% 5. Conclusion We introduced Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that enables frozen LLM agents to consolidate instructional videos into structured tutorialbook memory accessed through TOC retrieval. Across VidLearn and second software-tutorial evaluation, TAL outperforms representative fine-tuning-free baselines and scales monotonically with the number of tutorials consumed. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of instructional videos as scalable resource for enabling LLM agents to continually learn without parameter updates.

Implementation and Evaluation Details A.1. Baseline and Experimental Configuration The existing RAG baseline cannot learn directly from raw video inputs and therefore operates on video transcripts rather than the videos themselves. We construct subtitle corpus from the tutorial videos and segment each subtitle stream into overlapping 220-token chunks with 50-token overlap, retaining metadata including the opening name and video title. The retrieval query concatenates the question and answer options. Retrieval is performed with hybrid pipeline consisting of BM25 and dense retriever (OpenAIs text-embedding-3-small) based on cosine similarity. Each retriever returns 30 candidates, whose ranked lists are fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). The top five fused chunks are then supplied to the answer model as evidence. For the Video-RAG variants, we caption each event frame and pair the caption with its local transcript. The caption-retrieval variant provides the top five retrieved text units, while the frame-aware variant additionally provides the corresponding frames. A.2. TAL Operations and Prompts Reflective revision of Gϕ. Gϕ maintains an external readwrite history Ht containing previously generated questions, their teaching events, and the frozen answer models outcomes. Before each round, it reflects on Ht1: questions answered correctly are treated as too easy and trigger harder, non-duplicate questions about the same event, while incorrectly answered questions are retained as knowledge gaps in the QA bank. The validated questions and outcomes are then written back to Ht to guide the next round. Thus, reflective revision updates the generators external state and prompt context across rounds rather than its parameters. P.1 Reflective revision of the question generator Hard rewrite mode: - Rewrite attempt: {attempt_idx} - The previous question was answered correctly by the validator model. - Generate ONE new and harder MCQ on the same event/frame. - Do not reuse the same stem, option set, or answer key. - Prefer move-order traps, concrete tactical refutations, or subtle plan selection. - Make distractors very plausible and close to the best move. - Previous question: {prev_q} Previous correct option: {prev_answer} Tutorialbook editing. After evaluating the current tutorialbook, TAL routes each failed QA to its implicated chapter. For each chapter, the editor examines the failed questions, correct and common-wrong answers, explanations, and evidence to identify missing or misleading knowledge. It then adds or corrects the relevant content while preserving useful existing material. The revised chapter is re-evaluated on the QA bank and committed only if exact-match accuracy strictly improves; otherwise, the previous chapter is restored. P.2 Stage II tutorialbook editor (Write operator) [system] You are refining chess tutorialbook chapter using failed quiz questions. Given the current chapter and failed questions, improve instructional quality and question traceability. Integrate missing knowledge into the most relevant existing sections whenever possible (opening ideas, move purpose, plans, tactical motifs, common mistakes). If needed, add new sections, but do not bloat the chapter. [user] Current chapter: {textbook} Failed questions (id/options/correct/common-wrong/hint/explanation/context): {failed_questions} Update the chapter to cover these gaps. Return JSON only. TOC retrieval. TAL serializes the tutorialbook tree as compact index containing each chapters category/subtheme/chapter path, ID, and summary. Given this index, the question, and its options, the frozen LLM selects up to three relevant chapter IDs in JSON. TAL validates the IDs and expands only those chapters into the answer context. This tree-based retrieval avoids reading the full tutorialbook or relying on embedding similarity, achieving 50.0% Recall@3 compared with 28.2% for dense retrieval  (Table 6)  . Each added video increases the compact TOC by approximately 240 tokens, corresponding to 0.024% of 1Mtoken context window. If the TOC eventually exceeds the available context, hierarchical or multi-stage TOC navigation provides natural extension. P.3 TOC retrieval [system] You choose the most relevant tutorialbook chapters for one chess MCQ. Only use the provided TOC. Return strict JSON only: {"chapter_ids": [up to ids], "confidence": number}. [user] Question: {question_text} Options: {options_text} Tutorialbook TOC: toc_1: category=... subtheme=... chapter=... summary=... toc_2: ... Return JSON only. A.3. Judge Behavior and Verification frozen LLM judge is used only as the Stage grounding gate. Given candidate QA pair and its local subtitle window, it determines whether the reference answer is supported by the lecturers explanation. manual audit of 50 judge decisions found 100% agreement with human checks, with all retained answers traceable to subtitle evidence. The judge does not score reported metrics: accuracy, difficulty filtering, and Stage II acceptance use exact MCQ matching, and an edit is retained only if QA-bank accuracy improves. All 110 held-out questions were independently checked by two people. A.4. Construction Cost At API prices of $0.50 per million input tokens and $3 per million output tokens, Gemini-3-Flash construction uses measured average of 245k input tokens and 88k output tokens over 102 calls per video. This corresponds to approximately $0.38 per video ($0.12 input and $0.26 output), or $0.03 per minute for an average video duration of 12.9 minutes. Construction is one-time cost, and the resulting tutorialbook can be reused across different answer models without reconstruction. 18 A.5. Robustness to Noisy or Irrelevant Videos Videos are collected automatically by video-search agent that queries topic keywords and selects the top-k highly viewed matches, providing lightweight relevance and popularity filter. As the corpus grows over 12/24/36/48 videos, Transcript-RAG test accuracy fluctuates from 42.7% to 38.2%, 43.6%, and 37.3%, whereas TAL improves from 48.2% to 57.3%, 61.8%, and 64.6% under the same video budgets. These results suggest that TAL can tolerate naturally occurring variation in source quality and relevance, although robustness to controlled corruptions remains an important direction for future work. B. VidLearn Details For each of the 12 classical openings  (Table 9)  , we issue the opening name as YouTube search query and download the top results, retaining instructional videos that (i) carry usable English subtitles, (ii) have titles topically relevant to the queried opening (verified by an LLM-based title-relevance audit), and (iii) are not duplicates within the same opening (deduplicated by video ID). After filtering, we obtain 72 videos in total (6 per opening; 4 for training and 2 held-out for testing). The filtered corpus spans 14.9 hours and 462K subtitle words across the 48 training videos, plus 7.7 hours and 262K words across the 24 held-out test videos (22.5 hours and 724K words in total). All videos in VidLearn are publicly hosted on YouTube. To respect content creators rights and YouTubes Terms of Service, we release only per-question metadata (video ID, timestamp, question, options, answer index, and verified rationale) along with the question-generation and validation code, sufficient for full reproduction. Raw video files will not be redistributed. Table 9: The 12 classical openings covered in VidLearn.

sections.content: C. Human Performance One of the motivations behind TAL is to move closer to how humans acquire knowledge: by learning directly from demonstrations and explanations, rather than only from parameter updates or interaction traces. To provide qualitative reference for this learning paradigm, we additionally collect human responses on the same held-out test questions and compare the resulting trend with that of TAL. To collect human responses under the same protocol used for TAL, we built an interactive evaluation interface  (Fig. 4)  that presents each test instance exactly as it is given to the model and enforces closed-book conditions (no engines, books, or web search). We answered the held-out test questions through this interface after watching Kv {12, 24, 36, 48} training videos, with each Kv condition completed in separate session. This small-scale reference is used only to check whether the same learning-from-videos trend observed for TAL also appears for human under the same protocol, and is not intended as statistically representative estimate of human performance. 19 Figure 4: Interactive user interface used for human evaluation. Figure 5: Comparison of learning curves on the held-out test set. Both the human and TAL (avg) curves rise with the number of demonstration videos, supporting the central premise that instructional videos provide meaningful learning signal for both humans and TAL. The two curves, however, differ in shape in ways that are informative for TALs design. Humans exhibit strong consolidation efficiency: by extracting shared underlying logic across stylistically and pedagogically diverse presentations of the same opening, they acquire the relevant knowledge from only handful of tutorialsoften single high-quality demonstration. This contrast highlights both current limitation and an opportunity for TAL. The limitation is that, under the same evaluation protocol, TALs accuracy remains below the human reference. The opportunity is that TALs curve scales monotonically with the number of demonstration videos in the regime tested: each additional video continues to inject useful structure into tutorial memory. This suggests that TALs ability can continue to grow as more tutorials are consumed. D. TrainTest Similarity Analysis To assess the risk of traintest leakage, we compute nearest-neighbor overlap statistics between each of the 110 held-out test questions and two reference pools: (i) the harvested question bank Qbank , consisting of 174 QA pairs generated by Stage from the training videos (hereafter referred to as training questions); and (ii) the set of all subtitle chunks extracted from the training videos. The subtitle pool comprises 2,564 chunks, obtained from the 48 training videos using chunk size of 220 tokens with 50-token overlap, followed by exact-text deduplication. For each test question, we report the maximum similarity to any candidate in each reference pool. All texts are normalized by lowercasing, stripping punctuation, and collapsing repeated whitespace. TF-IDF features are extracted with unigrams and bigrams (ngram_range=(1,2)); for latent semantic similarity, we project the TF-IDF vectors into 128-dimensional subspace via TruncatedSVD and compute cosine similarity after L2 normalization. For each metric, we report the meanSD, the bootstrap 95% confidence interval (3,000 resamples at the question level, seed=7), the median, the 90th percentile (P90), and the proportion of test questions with similarity score 0.8, which serves as near-duplicate indicator. Online Self-Evolution The TAL tutorial memory framework supports not only offline construction from fixed video collection, but also on-demand expansion. When the online-learning mode is enabled, the agent inspects the Table of Contents (TOC) of the current memory upon receiving target topic (e.g., the name of an opening); if no matching entry is found in the TOC, the topic is treated as knowledge gap, and the agent generates set of search queries to retrieve relevant instructional videos from external sources such as YouTube. The retrieved videos are then processed through the same Stage and Stage II refinement pipeline used during initial construction. This can be viewed as lightweight closed loopkeyword gap detection video discovery memory updatewhich lets the memory grow without any parameter update. We exercise this mode end-to-end in our VidLearn experiments: the agent is given only the names of the 12 openings, without any pre-curated corpus or human-filtered video list, and constructs its entire training corpus through the TOC-based gap-detection mechanism alone. TAL therefore does not depend on manually curated sources; the framework itself can extend its knowledge base in open environments, leaving room for deployment to broader and faster-changing domains.
